newsitem.title: USA: Colombians in Miami lament drugs blacklisting.
newsitem.headline: Colombians in Miami lament drugs blacklisting.

text.p: Colombians in Miami expressed disappointment on Friday at the U.S decision to keep their country on a U.S. drugs blacklist, saying it would hurt and discourage ordinairy people who were not involved in the narcotics trade.
"I'm sad to see it. I am disappointed but not surprised," said Alfredo Quintero, a banker who is president of Miami's Colombian-American Chamber of Commerce.
"I think Colombia has made a major effort but it's not something you can change in a year," he told Reuters.
The United States announced on Friday it was again denying Colombia certification as an ally in the fight against drugs.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said corruption was rampant at the highest levels of the Colombian government and senior officials failed to cooperate with the United States.
"This is a decision that will hurt every Colombian," Quintero said. "My worry is that sooner or later they will stop caring."
It was likely to create an anti-American feeling, which would be counter-productive, he added.

Miami has a large Colombian community. Colombian and other Latin American businessmen in the city, gateway to trade with the region, had formed a Coalition to Certify Colombia to back the Bogata government as it pleaded its case to Washington.
The coalition's leader, Celestina de Tobon, said the threat that economic sanctions could be imposed at some stage now hung like "Damocles sword" over trade relations between Colombia and Florida.
"It would have an impact on Florida. Trade is $3.5 billion dollars per year," she said.
Colombia is one of south Florida's main trading partners and the coalition says 15,000 jobs here depend on the relationship.
Miami is also the main entry point for cocaine into the United States and narcotics agents call it the "command and control center" of the Colombian cocaine cartels' operations.
De Tobon, a financial consultant, said the decision against recertifying Colombia was made for political, not practical reasons. Poor Colombians could be driven into the arms of drug gangs.
It also reinforced negative stereotypes of Colombians.
"As Colombians and Colombian Americans, we have to continue living here and maintaining relations. The Coaliton will keep on fighting," she said.
Ambler Moss, director of the North-South Centre at the University of Miami and a former U.S. ambassador to Panama, said he thought the decision was a huge mistake.
"It is likely to be counterproductive and seen by Latin America as arrogant and hypocritical to single out Colombia."

He also said that the government had made a big effort, stiffening penalties for traffickers and reintroducing an extradition bill into the Colombia Congress. The Colombian private sector and the military and police fighting narcotics trafficking would be discouraged, he said.

The main problem of drugs in the United States was its own demand, he said, adding: "Ironically, there is nobody to decertify the United States, because only this country takes upon itself the arrogant attitude of decertifying others."
The practical impact would be minimal unless it is accompanied with economic sanctions "but it's a symbolic thing that really hurts," he said.
